input.question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?
input.ground_truth: The main reason is that electricity usage is highest during heat waves, because everyone's air conditioning is running at full blast. There's a second less important reason, which is that fossil fuel and nuclear power plants are less efficient in hot weather. They use outside air and/or water to cool their steam back to water to recycle back into the plant, and that doesn't work as well on a hot day. In fact, it turns out there's a theorem of thermodynamics that says that the maximum possible efficiency of both heat engines (power plant) and refrigerators (air conditioners) is worse when the outside air is warmer. _URL_0_

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine it’s a really, really hot day. Everyone turns on their air conditioners to stay cool. Air conditioners, TVs, fans, and even lights all need electricity to work. When it’s super hot, almost everyone wants to use their air conditioners at the same time.

But sometimes, the big power lines and machines that bring us electricity can’t carry all that electricity to everyone at once, especially if they get too hot or if something goes wrong. So, to keep the machines from breaking, the people who take care of the electricity have to turn off the power for some people for a little while. That’s what a blackout is—a time when the electricity goes off for some places.

So, when it’s extremely hot, too many people want electricity at the same time, and sometimes the system gets too busy and has to take a break, causing a blackout.
